questions.q: What does `accept()` actually return on the server side of a TCP connection?
options: A brand-new socket file descriptor dedicated to the newly connected client, distinct from the original listening socket
The same listening socket, reused for the new client's traffic
A string containing the client's IP address
Nothing -- accept() has no return value
questions.explain: accept() blocks until a client connects, then hands back a new file descriptor for that specific connection; the original listen_fd keeps listening for additional clients.

questions.q: Why does the client-side code only need `connect()`, not `bind()`/`listen()`/`accept()`?
options: Those three calls set up a socket to RECEIVE incoming connections, which only the server side needs to do; the client is initiating one specific outgoing connection
Clients are not allowed to use bind(), listen(), or accept() under any circumstances
connect() internally calls bind(), listen(), and accept() automatically
TCP clients never need a socket at all
questions.explain: bind/listen/accept prepare a socket to wait for and accept incoming connections -- the server's job. A client already knows who it's connecting to, so it just calls connect().

questions.q: Why is TCP described as a 'byte stream' with no preserved message boundaries?
options: send() and recv() calls don't correspond 1:1 -- bytes from multiple sends can arrive combined in one recv(), or one send's bytes can be split across multiple recv() calls
TCP always delivers exactly one send() per one recv(), with guaranteed message boundaries
TCP never guarantees that bytes arrive in order
Byte stream behavior only happens over slow or unreliable networks
questions.explain: TCP guarantees ordered bytes, not preserved message groupings -- a server's single recv() call can return parts of multiple sends, or only part of one, in any combination.

questions.q: Why is treating one recv() call as 'one message' described as a bug that 'works by accident' in testing?
options: Small, fast, local test connections rarely split messages across recv() calls, so the bug stays hidden until real network conditions (latency, fragmentation, load) actually cause a split
recv() always behaves identically regardless of network conditions
This assumption is actually always correct and never a bug
Testing environments use a completely different network protocol than production
questions.explain: The byte-stream nature of TCP means message splitting CAN happen any time -- it's just statistically rare on fast local test connections, which is exactly why the bug surfaces unpredictably in production instead of being caught early.

questions.q: Why must every socket call's return value be checked, rather than relying on C++ exceptions to signal failure?
options: Socket failures (disconnects, port conflicts, network errors) are reported through a negative return value and errno, not through C++ exceptions
Socket calls never fail in practice, so checking is just defensive style with no real purpose
C++ exceptions are thrown automatically by every socket call on failure
Checking return values is purely a style preference with no functional consequence
questions.explain: The sockets API is a C API -- it signals failure via return value and the global errno variable, never via a thrown C++ exception, so skipping the check means silently missing real failures.
